title: Types of issue
blurb: Name and recognise the issue types the QRG lists and know how each one is usually handled.
question: A delivered product fails one of its quality specifications, but the project board is happy to accept it as it is. What type of issue is this, and what is the acceptance called?

teach.body: The PRINCE2 7 quick reference guide (QRG) lists six types of issue. A problem has an immediate, negative impact. A concern still needs its timing and impact assessed. An event external to the project may affect it in some way. A business opportunity has unanticipated positive consequences for the project or the user organization. A request for change proposes a change to a baseline. An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications.

teach.body: A business opportunity is an issue, not a risk: it has already appeared, and it brings unanticipated positive consequences for the project or the user organization. An event external to the project comes from outside it, such as a new regulation or a market change, and may affect the project in some way. Both are captured and assessed like any other issue, so the project can decide whether to act.

teach.caption: Requests for change, off-specifications, business opportunities and problems or concerns needing formal review can each be described in an issue report.

teach.body: Northbrook Community Health is building an online outpatient booking service. In one week project manager Sanjay Mehta captures: the test server failing (a problem); a rumoured move of the lead tester (a concern); new accessibility guidance from a national standards body (an external event); the clinic managers asking for text-message reminders (a request for change); and a delivered booking screen that misses its response-time specification (an off-specification). Senior user Grace Owusu, acting as the change authority the board appointed, later grants a concession for the slower screen.

teach.text: Classic traps: a business opportunity is an ISSUE, not a risk opportunity (a risk opportunity is uncertain). A request for change is something someone wants to be different; an off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications. A concession is the acceptance of an off-specification without corrective action.

items: The QRG lists six types: problem, concern, event external to the project, business opportunity, request for change, off-specification.
Problem: immediate and negative. Concern: timing and impact still to be assessed.
Business opportunity: unanticipated positive consequences; it is an issue, not a risk.
Request for change: a proposal for a change to a baseline.
Off-specification: a product that will not meet its quality specifications; it may be accepted by concession.

summary: You can now name the issue types the QRG lists and recognise each from a short description. You also know that requests for change and off-specifications go through change control, and that an accepted off-specification is a concession.

A.q: Which issue type is a proposal for a change to a baseline?
A.why: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline (manual 10.1).

whyNot.0: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications.
whyNot.2: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed.
whyNot.3: A business opportunity has unanticipated positive consequences; it is not itself a proposal to change a baseline.

A.q: An issue is having an immediate and negative impact on the project. Which issue type is it?
A.why: A problem is an issue with an immediate and negative impact.

whyNot.0: A concern is one whose timing and impact still need to be assessed.
whyNot.1: An external event comes from outside the project and may affect it; the defining feature here is the immediate negative impact.
whyNot.3: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline.

A.q: Which issue type describes a product that will not meet its quality specifications?
A.why: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications.

whyNot.0: A request for change is a proposal for a change to a baseline.
whyNot.1: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact need to be assessed.
whyNot.2: A problem is an issue with an immediate negative impact; a product falling short of its specification has its own type.

B.q:
Which two statements about issue types are correct?
1. A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need to be assessed.
2. A business opportunity is recorded in the risk register as an opportunity.
3. An off-specification may be accepted without corrective action by a concession.
4. A request for change describes a product that has failed its quality check.
B.why: A concern still needs its timing and impact assessed (1), and an off-specification accepted without corrective action is a concession (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: a business opportunity is an issue, not a risk.
whyNot.2: Both are false: a business opportunity is an issue, and a product failing its specification is an off-specification.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: a failed product is an off-specification; a request for change is a proposal to change a baseline.

B.q: A national regulator announces a rule change, outside the project's control, that may affect one of the project's products. Which issue type is this?
B.why: An event external to the project that may affect it in some way is one of the issue types the QRG lists.

whyNot.0: Nobody has yet proposed a change to a baseline; the event comes first and any change would follow assessment.
whyNot.1: No product has been found to fall short of its quality specifications.

B.q: Early user testing shows that a product being built could also serve a second department, a benefit nobody had anticipated. Which issue type is this?
B.why: A business opportunity is an issue representing unanticipated positive consequences for the project or the user organization.

whyNot.0: A concern is an issue whose timing and impact still need assessing; the defining feature here is the unexpected upside.
whyNot.1: The finding comes from the project's own testing, not from outside the project.
whyNot.3: No product is falling short of its quality specifications.

C.q: A delivered training course will not meet one of its quality specifications. The project board agrees to accept it as it is. Which issue type is this, and what is the acceptance called?
C.why: A product that will not meet its quality specifications is an off-specification, and accepting it without corrective action is a concession.

whyNot.0: Nobody is proposing to change the baseline; the product simply falls short, which makes it an off-specification.
whyNot.1: The change budget funds approved changes; it is not the name for accepting a shortfall.
whyNot.2: Accepting the product as it is means no corrective action is taken.

C.q: A team manager reports that the only test rig has broken today and work has stopped. Which issue type is this, and what should happen first?
options: Problem; capture it and assess its impact
Concern; record it as a risk to monitor
External event; refer it to the business
C.why: A breakdown with immediate negative impact is a problem, and the technique starts by capturing it and assessing its impact on the project.

whyNot.1: It has already happened with a known negative impact, so it is a problem and an issue, not a risk.
whyNot.2: No product is falling short of its specification, and a concession is not a first step.
whyNot.3: The breakdown is inside the project and stops project work, so the project handles it.

C.q: Which pairing of issue type and handling is correct?
options: Business opportunity: recorded in the risk register as an opportunity
Request for change: goes through change control before any baseline change
Off-specification: handled through the quality register, not change control
Concern: escalated straight to the business layer for a decision
C.why: A request for change proposes a change to a baseline, so it must be assessed and decided through change control first.

whyNot.0: A business opportunity is an issue, captured and assessed through the issues practice.
whyNot.2: An off-specification is a discrepancy between the baseline and delivered products and must go through change control.
whyNot.3: A concern is first assessed; escalation follows only if a decision is beyond delegated authority or tolerance.

reteach.title: The wedding planner's folders
reteach.question: How would a wedding planner sort six different surprises into the right folders?

blocks.body: The caterer's van has broken down this morning (problem). The best man might be posted abroad (concern). The council closes the road outside the venue (external event). The venue offers a free garden upgrade (business opportunity). The couple want to add a ceilidh band to the agreed plan (request for change). The cake arrives in the wrong colour and the couple decide to keep it anyway (off-specification, accepted by concession).

blocks.text: Wanting something different is a request for change. Getting a product that will not meet its quality specifications is an off-specification.

explain.body: A problem is already hurting the project now. A concern is something whose timing and impact the project still needs to work out.

test.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a problem from a concern?
options: A concern has immediate negative impact; a problem still needs assessing
A problem has immediate negative impact; a concern still needs assessing
A problem is raised by the board; a concern is raised by the team
A problem goes in the daily log; a concern goes in the issue register
test.why: A problem has an immediate and negative impact; a concern is an issue whose timing and impact need to be assessed.

whyNot.2: Either type can be raised by anyone; the difference is the impact and its timing.
whyNot.3: Formal or informal handling depends on the issue, not on whether it is a problem or a concern.

explain.body: A request for change is a proposal to change a baselined product. An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specifications. Both go through change control.

rows.label: Example
values: Add a language to the site

test.q: The senior user asks for an extra language to be added to an approved website product. Which issue type is this?
test.why: Asking to alter an approved, baselined product is a request for change.

whyNot.0: Nothing is falling short of its specification; the senior user wants something different.
whyNot.1: There is no immediate negative impact; this is a proposal.
whyNot.2: The proposal is clear; it is not an issue whose timing and impact are unknown.

explain.body: A business opportunity is an issue that brings unanticipated positive consequences. The risk practice deals with uncertain opportunities; once something has appeared, it is an issue.

test.q: Where is a business opportunity handled in PRINCE2 7?
options: In the issues practice, as a type of issue
In the risk practice, as an opportunity
In the business case, as a dis-benefit
In the benefits approach, as a benefit
test.why: A business opportunity is one of the issue types, so it is captured and assessed in the issues practice.

whyNot.1: Risk opportunities are uncertain future events; a business opportunity is an issue.
whyNot.2: A dis-benefit is a negative outcome, not an opportunity.
whyNot.3: It may lead to new benefits later, but it is first captured and assessed as an issue.

explain.body: Problem, concern, external event, business opportunity, request for change, off-specification. A threat is a risk term, not an issue type.

items.label: issue types listed in the QRG
go through change control by definition

test.q: Which is NOT one of the PRINCE2 7 issue types?
test.why: A threat is an uncertain event with a negative impact on objectives, which is a risk term, not an issue type.

whyNot.0: A problem is an issue type with an immediate and negative impact.
whyNot.1: A concern is an issue type whose timing and impact need assessing.
whyNot.3: An off-specification is an issue type: a product that will not meet its quality specifications.
